paragraphs: Omega Healthcare Investors, Inc. ("Parent") is a Maryland corporation that invests in healthcare-related real estate properties located in the United States ("U.S."), the United Kingdom ("U.K.") and Canada, which investments comprise our one reportable segment. Omega became a publicly traded company listed on the New York Stock Exchange in 1992. Our primary objective is to provide strong returns to our investors, while serving as the preferred capital partner to our third-party healthcare operating companies and affiliates (collectively, our "operators") and other third-party high quality healthcare operators so they can concentrate on providing a high level of care for their resident-patients.

Parent, together with its consolidated subsidiaries (collectively, "Omega" or "Company") has elected to be taxed as a REIT for federal income tax purposes. Omega is structured as an umbrella partnership REIT ("UPREIT") under which all of Omega's assets are owned directly or indirectly by, and all of Omega's operations are conducted directly or indirectly through, its operating partnership subsidiary, OHI Healthcare Properties Limited Partnership (collectively with subsidiaries, "Omega OP"). As of December 31, 2025, Parent owned approximately 95% of the issued and outstanding units of partnership interest in Omega OP ("Omega OP Units"), and other investors owned approximately 5% of the outstanding Omega OP Units.

Our investment portfolio primarily consists of skilled nursing facilities ("SNFs"), assisted living facilities ("ALFs"), including care homes in the U.K., independent living facilities ("ILFs"), rehabilitation and acute care facilities ("specialty facilities") and continuing care retirement communities ("CCRCs"). The following is a summary of our various property types.

● Skilled nursing facilities – SNFs provide services that include daily nursing, therapeutic rehabilitation, social services, activities, housekeeping, nutrition, medication management and administrative services for individuals requiring certain assistance for activities in daily living.

● Assisted living facilities – ALFs provide services that include assistance for activities in daily living and permit residents to maintain some of their privacy and independence as they do not require constant supervision and assistance. Services usually include daily housekeeping, laundry, medical reminders and assistance with the activities of daily living, such as eating, dressing and bathing. Included within ALFs are Care Homes in the U.K., which are rental properties that provide similar services to ALFs in the U.S.

● Independent living facilities – ILFs are age-restricted multi-family properties with central dining facilities that provide services that include security, housekeeping, activities, nutrition and limited laundry services.

● Specialty facilities – Specialty facilities consist of specialty hospitals, long-term acute care hospitals, inpatient rehabilitation facilities, behavioral health substance facilities, behavioral health psychiatric facilities, traumatic brain injury facilities and other healthcare facilities.

● Continuing care retirement communities – CCRCs are retirement communities that include independent living, assisted living, memory care and skilled nursing units to provide a continuum of care in an integrated campus.

We maintain a portfolio of long-term healthcare facilities, mortgages and other real estate loans on healthcare facilities located in the U.S., the U.K. and Canada. Our investments are generally geographically diverse and operated by a diverse group of operators or third-party managers that we believe meet our standards for quality and experience of management and creditworthiness. Our criteria for evaluating potential investments include but are not limited to:
the quality and experience of management and the creditworthiness of the operator or manager of the facility;
the facility's historical and forecasted cash flow, its ability to meet operational needs, capital expenditure requirements and lease or debt service obligations and its prospects for growth;
the construction quality, condition and design of the facility and its environmental impact;
the location of the facility; the tax, growth, regulatory and reimbursement environment of the applicable jurisdiction;

headings: Risks Related to the Operators of Our Facilities
The bankruptcy or insolvency of our operators could limit or delay our ability to recover on our investments.
Failure by operators to comply with government regulations may adversely impact their ability to make debt or lease payments or meet their obligations to us.
We may be unable to find a replacement operator for one or more of our leased properties.
Uninsured losses or losses in excess of our operators' insurance coverage could adversely affect our financial position and our cash flow.
Our development and redevelopment projects may not yield anticipated returns.

We are exposed to operational risks with respect to our properties managed in RIDEA structures that could have a material adverse effect on our business, results of operations and financial condition.
Risks Related to Us and Our Operations
There are no assurances of our ability to pay dividends in the future.
We may be subject to additional risks in connection with our acquisitions of long-term care facilities.
Our assets, including our real estate and loans, are subject to impairment charges, and our valuation and reserve estimates are based on assumptions and may be subject to adjustment.
Our indebtedness could adversely affect our financial condition.
Covenants in our debt documents limit our operational flexibility, and a covenant breach could materially adversely affect our operations.
We are subject to particular risks associated with real estate ownership, which could result in unanticipated losses or expenses.
Our real estate investments are relatively illiquid, and we may not be able to acquire or dispose of properties or otherwise redeploy capital when desired or on favorable terms.
We face possible risks and costs associated with severe weather conditions, natural disasters or the physical effects of climate change.
As an owner or lender with respect to real property, we may be exposed to possible environmental liabilities.

The industry in which we operate is highly competitive. Increasing investor interest in our sector and consolidation at the operator or REIT level could increase competition and reduce our profitability.
Ownership of property outside the U.S. may subject us to different or greater risks than those associated with our U.S. investments, including currency fluctuations.
Our assets are concentrated in the long-term care industry and face geographic and operator concentration risk.
Our primary assets are the units of partnership interest in Omega OP and, as a result, we will depend on distributions from Omega OP to pay dividends and expenses.
Members of our management and Board hold partnership interests in Omega OP, and their interests may differ from those of our public stockholders.
paragraphs: This section discusses material risk factors that may affect our business, operations and financial condition. It does not describe all risks and uncertainties applicable to us, our industry or ownership of our securities. If any of the following risks, or any other risks and uncertainties that are not addressed below or that we have not yet identified, actually occur, we could be materially adversely affected and the value of our securities could decline.

Our financial position could be weakened and our ability to make distributions and fulfill our obligations with respect to our indebtedness could be limited if our operators (which reference, throughout this section, includes our TRS entities when we use a RIDEA structure and our managers, unless otherwise noted), or a portion thereof, become unable to meet their obligations to us or fail to renew or extend their relationship with us as their lease terms expire or their mortgages mature, or if we become unable to lease or re-lease our facilities or make mortgage loans on economically favorable terms. We have no operational control over our operators and limited contractual rights against our managers.

We are exposed to the risk that a distressed or insolvent operator may not be able to meet its lease, loan, mortgage or other obligations to us or other third parties. This risk is heightened during a period of economic or political instability. Although our lease and loan agreements typically provide us with the right to terminate, evict an operator, foreclose on our collateral, demand immediate payment and exercise other remedies upon the bankruptcy or insolvency of an operator, title 11 of the U.S. Code (the "Bankruptcy Code") would limit or, at a minimum, delay our ability to collect unpaid pre-bankruptcy rents and mortgage payments and to pursue other remedies against a bankrupt operator.

Leases. A bankruptcy filing by one of our lessee operators would typically prevent us from collecting unpaid pre-bankruptcy rents or evicting the operator, absent approval of the bankruptcy court. The Bankruptcy Code provides a lessee with the option to assume or reject an unexpired lease within certain specified periods of time. Generally, a lessee is required to pay all rent that becomes payable between the date of its bankruptcy filing and the date of the assumption or rejection of the lease (although such payments will likely be delayed as a result of the bankruptcy filing). If one of our lessee operators chooses to assume its lease with us, the operator must promptly cure all monetary defaults existing under the lease (including payment of unpaid pre-bankruptcy rents) and provide adequate assurance of its ability to perform its future lease obligations. Even where a lessee operator assumes its lease with us, it will first often threaten to reject that lease to obtain better lease terms from us, and we sometimes have to consider making, or we do make, such economic concessions to avoid rejection of the lease and our taking a closed facility back. If one of our lessee operators opts to reject its lease with us, we would have a claim against such operator for unpaid and future rents payable under the lease, but such claim would be subject to a statutory "cap" under the Bankruptcy Code, and would likely result in a recovery substantially less than the face value of such claim. Although the operator's rejection of the lease would permit us to recover possession of the leased facility, we would likely face losses, costs and delays associated with repairs and/or maintenance of the facility and then re-leasing the facility to a new operator, or costs associated with selling the facility. In any event, re-leasing a facility or selling it could take a material amount of time, and the pool of interested and qualified tenants or buyers will be limited due to the unique nature of our properties, which may depress values and our eventual recovery. Finally, whether a lease operator in bankruptcy ends up assuming or rejecting our lease, we will incur legal and collection costs, which can be difficult or impossible to recover.

Several other factors could impact our rights under leases with bankrupt operators. First, the operator could seek to assign its lease with us to a third party. The Bankruptcy Code disregards anti-assignment provisions in leases to permit the assignment of unexpired leases to third parties (provided all monetary defaults under the lease are promptly cured and the assignee can demonstrate its ability to perform its obligations under the lease). Second, in instances in which we have entered into a master lease agreement with an operator that operates more than one facility, the bankruptcy court could determine that the master lease was comprised of separate, divisible leases (each of which could be separately assumed or rejected), rather than a single, integrated lease (which would have to be assumed or rejected in its entirety). Finally, the bankruptcy court could re-characterize our lease agreement as a disguised financing arrangement, which could require us to receive bankruptcy court approval to foreclose or pursue other remedies with respect to the facility.

Mortgages and Secured Loans. A bankruptcy filing by an operator to which we have made a loan secured by a mortgage or other collateral would typically prevent us from collecting unpaid pre-bankruptcy mortgage payments and foreclosing on our collateral, absent approval of the bankruptcy court. As an initial matter, we could ask the bankruptcy court to order the operator to make periodic payments or provide other financial assurances on secured loans to us during the bankruptcy case (known as "adequate protection"), but the ultimate decision regarding "adequate protection" (including the timing and amount of any "adequate protection" payments) rests with the bankruptcy court. In addition, we would need bankruptcy court approval before commencing or continuing any foreclosure action against the operator's collateral (including a facility). The bankruptcy court could withhold such approval, especially if the operator can demonstrate that the facility or other collateral is necessary for an effective reorganization and that we have a sufficient "equity cushion" in the facility or that we are otherwise protected from any diminution in value of the collateral. If the bankruptcy court does not either grant us "adequate protection" or permit us to foreclose on our collateral, we may not receive any loan payments until after the bankruptcy court confirms a plan of reorganization for the operator. In addition, in any bankruptcy case of an operator to which we have made a loan, the operator may seek bankruptcy court approval to pay us (i) over a longer period of time than the terms of our loan, (ii) at a different interest rate, and/or (iii) for only the value of the collateral, instead of the full amount of the loan. Finally, even if the bankruptcy court permits us to foreclose on the facility, we would still be subject to the losses, costs and other risks associated with a foreclosure sale, including possible successor liability under government programs, indemnification obligations and suspension or delay of third-party payments. Should such events occur, our income and cash flow from operations would be adversely affected.

headings: Allowance for Credit Losses on Real Estate Loans, Non-real Estate Loans and Direct Financing Leases
paragraphs: Omega Healthcare Investors, Inc. ("Parent") is a Maryland corporation that, together with its consolidated subsidiaries has elected to be taxed as a REIT for federal income tax purposes. Omega is structured as an umbrella partnership REIT ("UPREIT") under which all of Omega's assets are owned directly or indirectly by, and all of Omega's operations are conducted directly or indirectly through, its operating partnership subsidiary, Omega OP. As of December 31, 2025, Parent owned approximately 95% of the issued and outstanding units of partnership interest in Omega OP ("Omega OP Units"), and other investors owned approximately 5% of the outstanding Omega OP Units.

Omega has one reportable segment consisting of investments in healthcare-related real estate properties located in the United States ("U.S."), the United Kingdom ("U.K.") and Canada. Our core business is to provide financing and capital to the long-term healthcare industry with a particular focus on skilled nursing facilities ("SNFs"), assisted living facilities ("ALFs") (including care homes in the U.K.), and to a lesser extent, independent living facilities ("ILFs"), rehabilitation and acute care facilities ("specialty facilities") and continuing care retirement community ("CCRCs"). Our core portfolio consists of our long-term leases and real estate loans with healthcare operating companies and affiliates (collectively, our "operators"). Real estate loans consist of mortgage loans and other real estate loans that are primarily collateralized by a first, second or third mortgage lien or a leasehold mortgage on, or an assignment of the partnership interest in the related properties. Additionally, during the fourth quarter of 2025, we began utilizing the structure authorized by the REIT Investment Diversification and Empowerment Act of 2007 (commonly referred to as "RIDEA"), whereby we own and operate healthcare facilities through third-party managers (collectively, our "managers"). In addition to our core investments, we make loans to operators and/or their principals. These loans, which may be either unsecured or secured by the collateral of the borrower, are classified as non-real estate loans. From time to time, we also acquire equity interests in joint ventures or entities that support the long-term healthcare industry and our operators, which may include ancillary service or technology companies, and in operating companies.

As of December 31, 2025, our portfolio of real estate investments consisted of 1,027 operating healthcare facilities (including properties associated with mortgages, assets held for sale and consolidated joint ventures), along with other real estate loans receivable (excluding mortgages) of $482.6 million and $414.1 million of investments in 15 unconsolidated entities. These healthcare facilities are located in 42 states, Washington, D.C., the U.K. and the Bailiwick of Jersey ("Jersey"), and are operated or managed by 89 third-party operators or managers. Our investment in these facilities, net of impairments and allowances, totaled approximately $10.5 billion at December 31, 2025, with approximately 98% of our real estate investments related to long-term healthcare facilities. Our portfolio is made up of (i) 561 SNFs, 339 ALFs, 19 ILFs, 16 specialty facilities and one CCRC, (ii) fixed rate mortgages on 47 SNFs, 42 ALFs and two ILFs and (iii) one property adjacent to one of our existing facilities that is held for sale. At December 31, 2025, our total investments also include non-real estate loans receivable of $330.3 million, consisting primarily of secured loans to third-party operators of our facilities.

As healthcare delivery continues to evolve, we continuously evaluate potential investments, our assets, operators and markets to position our portfolio for long-term success. As part of our evaluation, we may from time to time consider selling or transitioning assets that do not meet our portfolio criteria.

Our operators continue to face a number of industry challenges, including staffing shortages in certain regions, which have persisted since the COVID-19 pandemic. In addition, our operators have been and continue to be adversely affected by inflation-related cost increases and may be adversely impacted by recently announced global tariffs, each of which may increase expenses, exacerbate labor shortages and increase labor costs, among other adverse impacts. Our operators also may be adversely impacted by immigration restrictions and changes to immigration enforcement policy to the extent they contribute to labor shortages. There continues to be uncertainty regarding the extent and duration of these impacts for those operators, particularly given uncertainty as to whether reimbursement increases from the federal government, the states and the U.K. will be effective in offsetting these incremental costs and lost revenues. In addition, there remains uncertainty as to the impact of recent and potential further regulatory changes, including the recent Medicaid changes in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act ("OBBBA") and potential further reforms to Medicaid or Medicare and other state regulatory initiatives. While the OBBBA does not directly lower reimbursements related to long term care providers, it may indirectly impact our operators to the extent states in which they operate reduce reimbursement levels generally. This may occur as a result of reduced Medicaid funds allocated by states to long-term care providers due to lower reimbursement levels for hospitals and other healthcare providers. We continue to monitor these reimbursement impacts as well as the impacts of other regulatory changes, as discussed below, which could have a material adverse effect on an operator's results of operations and financial condition, which could adversely affect the operator's ability to meet its obligations to us. See "Government Regulation and Reimbursement" for additional information. While we continue to believe that longer term demographics will drive increasing demand for needs-based skilled nursing care, we remain cautious as some of the long-term impacts noted above may continue to have an impact on certain of our operators and their financial conditions.

paragraphs: Omega Healthcare Investors, Inc. ("Parent") 為一間馬裏蘭州公司，投資於美國 ("U.S.")、英國 ("U.K.") 和加拿大之醫療相關不動產，此投資為我們唯一應報告分部。Omega 於 1992 年成為公開上市公司，並於紐約證券交易所上市。我們的主要目標為提供優良回報給投資人，同時作為我們第三方醫療營運公司及關係企業 (合稱為 "operators") 及其他第三方高品質醫療營運公司之首選資金夥伴，使其能專注於為其住民患者提供高水平照護。

Parent 連同其合併子公司 (合稱為 "Omega" 或 "Company") 已選擇以 REIT 稅制進行美國聯邦所得稅之課稅。Omega 組織結構為一間傘型合夥 REIT ("UPREIT")，在此結構下，Omega 所有資產皆直接或間接由其營運合夥子公司 OHI Healthcare Properties Limited Partnership 所擁有，且 Omega 所有營運皆直接或間接透過該營運合夥子公司進行 (合稱為 "Omega OP")。截至 2025 年 12 月 31 日，Parent 持有約 95% 之 Omega OP 發行在外之合夥權益單位 ("Omega OP Units")，其他投資人則持有約 5% 之發行在外 Omega OP Units。
我們之投資組合主要為護理之家 ("SNFs")、輔助生活設施 ("ALFs")，包括英國之護理之家、獨立生活設施 ("ILFs")、復健及急性照護設施 ("特殊設施") 及持續照護退休社區 ("CCRCs")。以下為我們各類不動產之總結。
● 護理之家 – SNFs 提供之服務包括每日護理、復健治療、社會服務、活動、清潔、營養、藥物管理及行政服務，以協助需協助日常活動之個人。
● 輔助生活設施 – ALFs 提供協助日常活動之服務，並讓住民維持部分隱私與獨立性，因其不需持續監督與協助。服務通常包括每日清潔、洗衣、醫療提醒及協助日常活動，例如進食、穿衣與沐浴。包含於 ALFs 中的英國護理之家，為出租性質之不動產，提供與美國 ALFs 相似之服務。
● 獨立生活設施 – ILFs 為限制年齡之多戶住宅，設有中央餐飲設施，提供之服務包括安全、清潔、活動、營養及有限洗衣服務。
● 特殊設施 – 特殊設施包括特殊醫院、長期急性照護醫院、住院復健設施、行為健康物質設施、行為健康精神科設施、腦部創傷設施及其他醫療設施。
● 繼續照護退休社區 – CCRCs 為退休社區，包含獨立生活、輔助生活、記憶照護及護理之家單位，以提供整合式校園內之連續照護。
我們持有美國、英國及加拿大等地之長期醫療設施、房貸及其他位於醫療設施之不動產貸款組合。我們之投資通常地理分佈多元，並由一羣多元之經營者或第三方管理人經營，我們認為這些經營者或管理人符合我們對管理品質與經驗及信用worthiness之標準。我們評估潛在投資之標準包括但不限於：
經營者或管理人之管理品質與經驗及信用worthiness；
該設施之歷史及預測現金流，其滿足營運需求、資本支出需求、租賃或債務服務義務之能力，以及其成長前景；
該設施之建設品質、狀況及設計，以及其環境影響；
該設施之位置；適用司法管轄區之稅收、成長、法規及補償環境；
該設施之佔用率及相同或附近社區中類似醫療設施之需求；

paragraphs: Omega Healthcare Investors, Inc. ("Parent") 為一間馬裏蘭州公司，已選擇以 REIT 稅制納稅，適用美國聯邦所得稅目的。Omega 組織架構為一間傘型合作夥伴 REIT ("UPREIT")，其所有資產皆直接或間接由 Omega OP 擁有，且所有營運皆直接或間接透過 Omega OP 進行。截至 2025 年 12 月 31 日，Parent 擁有約 95% 的 Omega OP 發行在外的單位權益 ("Omega OP Units")，其他投資者則擁有約 5% 的 Omega OP Units。

Omega 有一個應報告分部，主要投資於美國 ("U.S.")、英國 ("U.K.") 和加拿大之醫療相關不動產。我們的核心業務為為長期醫療產業提供融資與資本，特別著重於護理之家 ("SNFs")、輔助生活設施 ("ALFs")（包括英國之護理之家），以及較少程度的獨立生活設施 ("ILFs")、復健與急性照護設施 ("特殊設施") 和持續照護退休社區 ("CCRCs")。我們的核心資產為與醫療營運公司及其關係企業 (合稱為 "營運者") 之長期租賃及不動產貸款。不動產貸款包括抵押貸款及其他不動產貸款，主要以第一、第二或第三順位抵押權或租賃抵押權或相關不動產之合夥權益讓與為擔保。此外，於 2025 年第四季，我們開始運用 2007 年 REIT 投資多元化與賦權法案 (常簡稱為 "RIDEA") 所授權之結構，透過第三方管理公司 (合稱為 "管理公司") 擁有並營運醫療設施。除了核心投資外，我們亦對營運者及其主要股東提供貸款。這些貸款可能為無擔保或以借款人之擔保品為擔保，歸類為非不動產貸款。我們偶爾也會取得與長期醫療產業及營運者相關之合資企業或實體之股權，可能包括輔助服務或科技公司，以及營運公司。

截至2025年12月31日，本公司之不動產投資組合包含1,027處營運中的醫療設施（包括與抵押貸款相關之不動產、待售資產及合併之合資企業），以及不包含抵押貸款之其他不動產貸款應收款$482.6百萬美元與$414.1百萬美元之15家未合併企業投資。這些醫療設施位於42個州、華盛頓特區、英國及澤西島（"Jersey"），並由89家第三方營運商或管理公司營運或管理。扣除減損與撥備後，本公司對這些設施之投資總計約為10.5十億美元，其中約98%之不動產投資與長期醫療設施相關。本公司之投資組合包含（i）561處長期照護機構（SNFs）、339處護理機構（ALFs）、19處機構護理設施（ILFs）、16處專業設施及一所持續照護退休社區（CCRC），（ii）47處SNFs、42處ALFs及2處ILFs之固定利率抵押貸款，以及（iii）一處位於本公司現有設施旁之待售不動產。截至2025年12月31日，本公司總投資亦包含$330.3百萬美元之非不動產貸款應收款，主要為對本公司設施之第三方營運商之擔保貸款。
隨著醫療服務交付持續演進，我們持續評估潛在投資、資產、營運者及市場，以期為長期成功定位投資組合。作為評估之一環，我們偶爾會考慮出售或轉移不符合我們投資組合標準之資產。

我們的營運者持續面臨多項產業挑戰，包括某些地區之人力短缺，此情況自 COVID-19 疫情以來持續存在。此外，營運者已並持續受到通貨膨脹相關成本增加之影響，且可能因最近宣佈之全球關稅而受到不利影響，這些因素可能增加成本、惡化人力短缺並提高人力成本，以及其他不利影響。營運者亦可能因移民限制及移民執法政策變更而受到不利影響，尤其在這些變更可能導致人力短缺之情況下。對於這些影響的範圍與持續時間仍存在不確定性，特別是因為不確定美國聯邦政府、各州及英國是否能透過提高補償金額來抵消這些額外成本與損失收入。此外，對於近期及潛在進一步的法規變更之影響仍存在不確定性，包括近期在「一項大而美好的法案」("OBBBA") 中的醫療補償變更，以及潛在進一步的醫療保險或醫療補助及其它州法規措施之改革。雖然 OBBBA 並未直接降低與長期照護提供者相關之補償金額，但可能間接影響營運者，尤其在營運者所處之州份可能降低補償金額。這可能發生在州政府因醫院及其他醫療提供者之補償金額降低而減少分配給長期照護提供者之醫療補助資金。我們持續監測這些補償影響及其他法規變更之影響，如後文所述，這些變更可能對營運者之營運結果與財務狀況造成重大不利影響，進而影響營運者履行對我們之義務之能力。請參閱 "政府法規與補償" 章節以取得更多資訊。雖然我們持續認為長期人口結構將驅動對需求導向之護理之家服務之需求增加，但我們仍謹慎，因上述部分長期影響可能持續影響我們部分營運者及其財務狀況。

headings: 與我們設施營運者相關的風險
我們營運者之破產或財務困難可能限制或延遲我們回收投資之能力。
營運者未能遵守政府規範，可能不利於其償還債務或租賃款項，或履行對我們之義務。
我們可能無法為我們租賃之不動產尋找替代營運者。
未投保之損失或損失超出營運者保險範圍，可能不利於我們之財務狀況與現金流。
我們之開發與重建專案可能無法達成預期回報。
我們對於透過 RIDEA 結構管理之不動產，面臨營運風險，可能對我們之業務、營運成果與財務狀況造成重大不利影響。
與我們及我們營運相關之風險
本公司無法保證未來有能力發放股息。
本公司可能因取得長期照護設施而面臨額外風險。
本公司資產，包括不動產及貸款，可能需提列減損費用，且本公司之評價及備抵估計係基於假設，可能需進行調整。
本公司負債可能對財務狀況造成不利影響。
債務契約限制本公司營運彈性，且違約契約可能對營運造成重大不利影響。
本公司因擁有不動產而面臨特定風險，可能導致未預期之損失或費用。
本公司不動產投資流動性較低，且可能無法在所期望之時間或有利條件下取得或處分不動產，或重新運用資本。
本公司可能因極端天氣、自然災害或氣候變遷之物理影響而面臨風險與成本。
作為不動產的所有人或貸款人，我們可能面臨環境責任的潛在風險。
我們所從事的產業具有高度競爭性。投資人對我們產業的興趣增加，以及在經營者或REIT層級的併購，可能會增加競爭並降低我們的獲利能力。
我們持有位於美國境外的不動產，可能會面臨與美國投資相關風險不同或更高的風險，包括貨幣波動。
我們的資產主要集中於長期照護產業，並面臨地理及經營者集中風險。
我們的主要資產為Omega OP的合夥權單位，因此我們將依賴Omega OP的分紅以支付股息及費用。
我們管理層及董事會成員持有Omega OP的合夥權單位，其利益可能與我們的公開股東不同。
paragraphs: 本節討論可能影響我們業務、營運及財務狀況的重大風險因素。並未說明所有適用於我們、我們產業或持有我們證券的風險與不確定性。若任何下列風險，或任何未在下文提及或尚未識別的其他風險與不確定性實際發生，我們可能受到重大不利影響，且我們證券的價值可能下跌。

我們的財務狀況可能受到削弱，且我們發放分紅及履行我們債務義務的能力可能受到限制，若我們的經營者（在本節中，若我們使用 RIDEA 結構，則包含我們的 TRS 企業，除非另有說明）或其部分，無法履行對我們的義務，或未能在租賃合約到期或抵押貸款到期時續約或延長與我們的關係，或我們無法以經濟上有利的條件租賃或重新租賃我們的設施，或無法以經濟上有利的條件發放抵押貸款。我們對經營者沒有實際的營運控制權，且對管理層的契約權利有限。

我們面臨的風險是，陷入財務困境或破產的經營者可能無法履行其對我們或其他第三方的租賃、貸款、抵押貸款或其他義務。此風險在經濟或政治不穩定時期會更加嚴重。儘管我們的租賃與貸款協議通常會給予我們終止租賃、驅逐經營者、對我們的擔保品進行拍賣、要求立即付款並行使其他救濟措施之權利，但美國法典第 11 編（「破產法」）會限制或至少延遲我們收取破產前租金與抵押貸款付款的能力，並限制我們對破產經營者追索其他救濟措施的能力。

租賃。我們的租賃承租人若提出破產聲請，通常會阻止我們收取破產前未支付的租金或驅逐該承租人，除非獲得破產法院的批准。破產法賦予承租人選擇在特定期間內承認或拒絕未到期租賃的權利。通常，承租人必須支付其破產聲請日與租賃承認或拒絕日之間產生的所有租金（儘管這些付款會因破產聲請而延遲）。若我們的租賃承租人選擇承認與我們的租賃，該承租人必須立即解決租賃下所有財務違約（包括支付未支付的破產前租金），並提供足夠的證據證明其未來履行租賃義務的能力。即使承租人承認與我們的租命，該承租人通常會先威脅拒絕租賃以獲得更好的租賃條款，我們有時必須考慮做出經濟讓步，以避免租賃被拒絕，以及我們收回封閉設施。若我們的租賃承租人選擇拒絕與我們的租賃，我們將對該承租人擁有未支付及未來租金的索賠，但此索賠將受到破產法規定的「上限」限制，且實際回收金額可能遠低於索賠金額。雖然承租人拒絕租賃將允許我們收回租賃設施的控制權，但我們將面臨修繕與/或維護設施的損失、成本與延遲，以及重新租賃設施給新承租人，或出售設施的相關成本。無論如何，重新租賃設施或出售設施可能耗費大量時間，且由於我們設施的獨特性，潛在的租戶或買家將有限，這可能壓低價值與我們最終的回收金額。最後，無論租賃承租人在破產中是否承認或拒絕我們的租賃，我們將產生法律與追討費用，這些費用可能難以或無法回收。

其他因素可能影響我們在與破產經營者租賃下的權利。首先，經營者可能尋求將其與我們的租賃轉讓給第三方。破產法忽略租賃中的反轉讓條款，允許未到期租賃轉讓給第三方（前提是所有租賃下的財務違約迅速解決，且受讓方能證明其履行租賃義務的能力）。其次，在我們與經營者簽訂主租賃協議，而該經營者經營多個設施的情況下，破產法院可能裁定該主租賃協議由多個可分割的租賃組成（每個租賃可獨立承認或拒絕），而非單一整合租賃（必須整體承認或拒絕）。最後，破產法院可能將我們的租賃協議重新歸類為隱蔽的融資安排，這可能要求我們在拍賣或追索其他救濟措施前獲得破產法院的批准。

抵押貸款與擔保貸款。我們的貸款人若提出破產聲請，通常會阻止我們收取破產前未支付的抵押貸款付款並對我們的擔保品進行拍賣，除非獲得破產法院的批准。首先，我們可以請求破產法院下令貸款人定期支付或提供其他財務保證，以確保我們的擔保貸款在破產程序中（稱為「足夠保護」）。然而，關於「足夠保護」（包括支付時間與金額）的最終決定權在於破產法院。此外，我們在開始或繼續對貸款人擔保品（包括設施）進行拍賣行動前，必須獲得破產法院的批准。破產法院可能拒絕此批准，特別是在貸款人能證明設施或其他擔保品對有效重組是必要的，且我們在設施中擁有足夠的「權益緩衝」，或我們在其他方面受到保護，以避免擔保品價值下降的情況下。若破產法院未授予我們「足夠保護」或允許我們對擔保品進行拍賣，我們可能在破產法院確認貸款人重組計劃前無法收到任何貸款付款。此外，在貸款人破產的情況下，貸款人可能請求破產法院批准我們（i）在貸款條款之外的較長時間內付款，（ii）以不同利率付款，以及/或（iii）僅支付擔保品價值，而非貸款總額。最後，即使破產法院允許我們對設施進行拍賣，我們仍將面臨拍賣銷售的損失、成本及其他風險，包括政府計畫下的繼承責任、賠償義務及第三方付款的中止或延遲。若發生上述情況，將對我們的收入與營運現金流產生不利影響。
